courses.summary: The incident response lifecycle (preparation, detection and analysis, containment/eradication/recovery, post-incident activity) and ready-to-run playbooks for ransomware, compromised accounts, malware on endpoints and lost devices - practised as ordered steps, scenarios and tickets.

lessons.title: The lifecycle, roles and severity

scenes.text: A file server shows files renamed with a strange extension. Isha is on call. The first twenty minutes decide whether this is an annoyance or a company-wide outage.
Your turn: read the key ideas, then apply them hands-on in the activity that follows.

steps.title: Lifecycle
steps.body: Widely taught (NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2) as four phases: **Preparation**; **Detection and Analysis**; **Containment, Eradication and Recovery**; **Post-Incident Activity** (lessons learned). In practice they loop: analysis continues during containment.

steps.title: Roles
steps.body: **Incident commander/manager** (decisions, comms cadence), **technical lead(s)**, **scribe** (timeline), **communications** (leadership, legal, HR, PR), **liaison** for external parties. Severity (e.g. SEV1-SEV4) is based on business impact, data sensitivity and spread.

steps.title: Preserve evidence
steps.body: Contain without destroying evidence: isolate network rather than power off when practical (volatile memory), snapshot VMs, preserve logs, keep a timestamped scribe log in UTC.

lessons.title: The lifecycle and CVSS

scenes.text: The weekly scan shows 4,213 findings. The CIO wants 'all critical fixed by Friday'. Meera asks Isha for a defensible priority order.
Your turn: read the key ideas, then apply them hands-on in the activity that follows.

steps.title: Lifecycle
steps.body: **Discover assets -> scan (authenticated where possible) -> prioritise -> remediate (patch/mitigate/accept) -> verify (rescan) -> report**. You cannot protect assets you do not know about; inventory is step zero.

steps.title: CVSS
steps.body: The Common Vulnerability Scoring System rates technical severity 0.0-10.0. Qualitative bands (v3.x/v4.0): **None 0.0, Low 0.1-3.9, Medium 4.0-6.9, High 7.0-8.9, Critical 9.0-10.0**. Base score is not risk: combine with exploitation evidence, asset criticality, exposure (internet-facing?) and compensating controls.

steps.title: Signals
steps.body: CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue lists flaws seen exploited in the wild; EPSS estimates the probability of exploitation in the next 30 days. Both help prioritise beyond CVSS.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Sorting purely by CVSS: a 9.8 on an isolated lab box may matter less than a 7.5 being actively exploited on an internet-facing server.

courses.title: Digital forensics basics: evidence, hashing and timelines
courses.summary: Forensic principles for first responders and analysts: order of volatility, chain of custody, cryptographic hashing for integrity, forensic copies, log-based timelines and clear reporting. Defensive and lawful use only.
outcomes: Apply the order of volatility
Maintain chain of custody and integrity (hashes)

lessons.title: Principles: volatility, custody, integrity

scenes.text: HR reports an employee has been leaking documents. The laptop is still on, logged in, on Wi-Fi. What do you touch first?
Your turn: read the key ideas, then apply them hands-on in the activity that follows.

steps.title: Order of volatility
steps.body: Collect the most volatile first: CPU registers/cache, **RAM**, network connections and ARP/routing tables, running processes, **disk**, remote logging/monitoring data, archival media. Powering off loses memory.

steps.title: Chain of custody
steps.body: A record of who handled evidence, when, why and where it was stored, from collection to court/closure. Evidence bags/labels, signed hand-overs, secure storage.

steps.title: Integrity
steps.body: Create a **forensic copy** (bit-for-bit image) and work on the copy; use a write blocker for physical disks; record **SHA-256** (not MD5 or SHA-1 alone) of original and copy. Matching hashes show the copy is identical; any changed bit changes the hash completely.

steps.title: Legal
steps.body: Only acquire evidence with proper authority (policy, consent or legal process). Involve legal/HR first for people-related cases.

steps.body: This course teaches detection, response and recovery. Practise only on systems and data you are authorised to examine. Hosts, users and addresses are invented (documentation ranges, contoso.local, example.com).

lessons.title: Lab: Monolith, modular monolith, microservices

steps.title: The spectrum
steps.body:
- **Monolith**: one deployable; simple ops, easy transactions; risk of a 'big ball of mud'
- **Modular monolith**: one deployable with enforced module boundaries
- **Microservices**: independently deployable services owning their data; scale teams and parts separately, but add network failures, eventual consistency, observability and platform cost

steps.title: Conway's law
steps.body: Systems mirror team communication structures. Split services along team and domain boundaries, not technical layers.

steps.title: Common mistakes

- Splitting before you understand the domain

lessons.title: Lab: SLIs, SLOs and error budgets

scenes.text: A team promises 99.999% for an internal dashboard and burns out on-call.
SLOs set by user needs and error budgets balance reliability and speed.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **SLI**: measured indicator (e.g. % of requests < 300 ms and non-5xx)
- **SLO**: target for the SLI over a window (99.9% over 30 days)
- **SLA**: contractual promise with penalties (looser than the SLO)
- **Error budget** = 1 − SLO

steps.title: Budget maths
steps.body: 99.9% over 30 days → 0.1% × 43,200 min = **43.2 minutes** of allowed unavailability.

steps.title: Mistakes
steps.body:
- 100% targets
- SLIs measured on servers only, not from the user's perspective

steps.title: Resilience patterns

Threshold 3 consecutive failures → open; while open, the next 2 calls are rejected ('reject'); then half-open: one trial call — ok → closed, fail → open again. activity.solution:
events = input().split()
state, fails, wait, out = 'closed', 0, 0, []
for e in events:
    if state == 'open':
        if wait > 0:
            wait -= 1; out.append('reject')
            if wait == 0: state = 'half-open'
            continue
    if state == 'half-open':
        if e == 'ok': state, fails = 'closed', 0
        else: state, wait = 'open', 2
        out.append(state); continue
    if e == 'ok': fails = 0
    else:
        fails += 1
        if fails >= 3: state, wait = 'open', 2
    out.append(state)
print(*out)

rounds.q: Explain the difference between a monolith and microservices and when you'd choose each.
rounds.model: A monolith is one deployable unit — simple to build, test and operate, with easy transactions. Microservices are independently deployable services that own their data, letting many teams scale and release separately, at the cost of network failures, eventual consistency and platform overhead. For a small team or uncertain domain I'd start with a modular monolith and extract services when team size or scaling needs justify it.
followups: How would you split an existing monolith?

rounds.q: How do you make an API endpoint safe to retry?
rounds.model: Make the operation idempotent: natural idempotency via PUT/DELETE, or an Idempotency-Key header whose first response is stored and replayed for repeats. Combine with unique constraints in the DB and return the same status/body for replays.
followups: How long do you keep keys?

rounds.q: What makes a good unit test?
rounds.model: It is fast, isolated from I/O, deterministic, tests one behaviour via the public interface with clear Arrange–Act–Assert, and covers boundaries and failure cases, not just the happy path.

rounds.q: Explain SOLID's dependency inversion with an example.
rounds.model: High-level code depends on abstractions, and concrete implementations are injected. A Notifier takes a Sender interface; production passes an SMTP sender, tests pass a fake. That decouples policy from details and makes testing easy.

import sys
from collections import Counter

SLOW_MS = 500

def classify(status, latency):
    if status == 0 or 500 <= status <= 599: return 'DOWN'
    if 200 <= status <= 299: return 'SLOW' if latency > SLOW_MS else 'OK'
    return 'WARN'

counts = Counter()
for ln in sys.stdin.read().split('\n'):
    if not ln.strip(): continue
    url, st, lat = ln.split()
    c = classify(int(st), int(lat)); counts[c] += 1
    print(url, c)

Clean code is code another engineer can read, change and test safely. The core habits:

- **Guard clauses** instead of deep nesting

activity.prompt: Refactor the smelly function `f` into a clean `shipping_cost(weight_kg, express)` that keeps EXACTLY the same behaviour: base 50, +10 per kg above 2 kg, express doubles the total. Read 'weight express(0/1)' and print the cost.

BASE_COST = 50
PER_EXTRA_KG = 10
FREE_KG = 2

def shipping_cost(weight_kg, express):
    extra_kg = max(0, weight_kg - FREE_KG)
    cost = BASE_COST + extra_kg * PER_EXTRA_KG
    return cost * 2 if express else cost

w, e = input().split()
print(shipping_cost(int(w), e == '1'))

steps.title: Debugging in production
steps.body: Use metrics (memory over time), logs, heap dumps/profilers (tracemalloc, py-spy, jmap/Eclipse MAT, Chrome heap snapshots), and compare snapshots.

steps.title: Sawtooth vs staircase
steps.body: Sawtooth memory (rises, GC drops it) is normal. A **staircase** that never returns to baseline is a leak.

steps.title: Don't
steps.body: Don't just raise the memory limit — it only delays the crash.

ticket.description: Alert: orders-api restarts 4x/day with OOMKilled. Latency spikes before each restart. Started after release 5.12 last Thursday.

investigate.label: Grafana: container memory over 24h
investigate.reveal: Memory climbs in a straight staircase from 300 MB to the 1 GiB limit, then the pod is killed.

investigate.label: Diff release 5.12
investigate.reveal: 5.12 added `PRICE_CACHE = {}` keyed by (sku, user_id, timestamp) with no eviction.

investigate.label: Check DB slow-query log
investigate.reveal: Normal; p95 18 ms.

investigate.label: Node CPU
investigate.reveal: CPU 35%, normal.

options: Unbounded in-process cache keyed with a timestamp, so entries never repeat or expire
diagnosis.why: Including the timestamp in the key makes every entry unique; without eviction memory grows until OOM.

resolution: Mitigate: roll back to 5.11 (or raise limit temporarily) and confirm restarts stop
Replace the dict with an LRU/TTL cache (maxsize, ttl) and drop timestamp from the key
Add a memory-growth alert on slope, not only on limit
Load test for 8h to confirm flat memory
Write the post-incident review

closure.model: Root cause: release 5.12 introduced an unbounded dict cache keyed by timestamp, so memory grew ~120 MB/h until OOMKill. Fix: rolled back, then shipped TTL-LRU cache (maxsize 10k, ttl 5 min) keyed by sku. Verification: 8h soak test flat at ~320 MB; no restarts in 48h.

steps.title: Races
steps.body: When two threads/processes read the same value, both modify, both write — one update is lost. Fixes: locks, atomic DB updates (`UPDATE … SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE qty > 0`), optimistic concurrency (version column), queues.

steps.body: `UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = 'X' AND qty > 0;` then check rows affected = 1.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding sleep to 'fix' timing
- Locking too broadly (kills throughput)

choices.feedback: Yes — a reliable repro makes the fix verifiable.

steps.title: Problem
steps.body: Line 1: n integers. Line 2: q. Next q lines: l r (0-based, inclusive). Print each range sum on its own line.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.body:
Prefix sums: pre[i+1] = pre[i] + a[i]; sum(l..r) = pre[r+1] - pre[l]

Build prefix once in O(n); every query is then O(1).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Off-by-one: use pre of length n+1 so pre[0] = 0.
- Recomputing the sum per query is O(n·q).

steps.title: Complexity
steps.body: Time **O(n)**, extra space **O(n)**. Say both out loud in an interview, then mention the brute force you rejected.

steps.title: Problem
steps.body: One line of integers (may be negative). Print the maximum sum of a non-empty contiguous subarray.

steps.title: Key idea
steps.body:
Kadane: cur = max(x, cur + x); best = max(best, cur)

At each element decide: extend the current run or start fresh.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Initialising best = 0 breaks all-negative input; start with the first element.

steps.title: Complexity
steps.body: Time **O(n)**, extra space **O(1)**. Say both out loud in an interview, then mention the brute force you rejected.

    best = max(best, cur)

steps.title: Key idea

Never move backwards in the text; on mismatch fall back via the failure table.
